competitors.name: Wheel of Names (wheelofnames.com)
competitors.model: Free, ad-supported (dismissible per-session), optional login for cloud save. Explicitly takes no payments or donations. Est. ~9.6M monthly visitors / ~19M visits.
competitors.note: The category default and the search-result winner. Genuinely good: 150+ sounds, weighted segments, images/Unsplash, Google Sheets import, 65 languages, physics-based spin, short share links. Weak: the page is an ad frame; cross-device saving needs an account; cloud wheels (including student names) are stored in Google Firestore; needs internet.

competitors.name: Picker Wheel (pickerwheel.com)
competitors.model: Freemium. Free tier = ads + 15 saved files. Personalized $5/mo ($60/yr), Professional $10/mo ($120/yr), Business $25/mo ($300/yr). Read live from pickerwheel.com/plan.
competitors.note: Best feature set on the web: Normal / Elimination / Accumulation modes, weighted entries, per-entry colors, image entries, Instagram comment import. Weak: everything meaningful is metered (15 files free, ad-free is paid, 3 AI queries/day), and persistence beyond browser cache requires an account.

competitors.name: Spin The Wheel - Random Picker (iOS, Taurius Petraitis)
competitors.model: Free with interstitial ads + IAP coin economy for the wheel library. 4.87★ / 93,693 ratings (iTunes API, 2026-08-09).
competitors.note: The #1 mobile app by a wide margin, and the one whose users praise 'you don't have to sign up for anything.' Weak: ads fire after you finish spinning, the 'recently spun' no-repeat list is broken per reviews, wheels have silently disappeared for users, and the library is gated behind a coin/ad-watching loop.

competitors.name: Spin Wheel Decisions (iOS, Aesthetic Apps & Widgets srl)
competitors.model: Was free/one-time-purchase, pivoted to subscription (~$3/week per reviews, one review cites $15/mo). 4.48★ / 18,902 ratings.
competitors.note: The cautionary tale, and our single best marketing contrast. Free tier now caps the wheel at ~5 options and 1 wheel; spin duration is paywalled. Its recent review page is a wall of 1-stars from long-time users who lost wheels they'd spent hours building.

competitors.name: Classroomscreen
competitors.model: Freemium. Basic free (all 26 widgets but only 3 saved name lists). Pro $3/mo or $36/yr. Organization $525/yr for 25 licenses. Read live from classroomscreen.com/pricing.
competitors.note: The real classroom incumbent — the name picker is one widget inside a whole projected teacher dashboard (timer, noise meter, work symbols). Weak for us to attack head-on; strong for us to be the better single-purpose tool the teacher opens when they don't want the whole dashboard. Free tier's 3-list cap bites any teacher with 5 sections.

competitors.name: Flippity Random Name Picker (flippity.net)
competitors.model: Completely free, Google Sheets-backed, no paid tier.
competitors.note: A genuine teacher staple. Spinner + single name + lineups + groups up to 15 + teams up to 15 — the group/team feature is a real gap in most wheel apps. Weak: requires a Google account, copying a template sheet, and publishing it; the setup is a multi-minute chore and the UI is visibly a decade old.

competitors.name: Popsicle/equity sticks in a cup, and =RANDBETWEEN in Sheets/Excel
competitors.model: Free. Already in the room. Zero setup, zero network, zero permission slip.
competitors.note: This is the actual competitor. Sticks never buffer, never show an ad, never need district approval, and visibly prove fairness because the class watches the hand go in the cup. Where they lose: rebuilding the cup each period, no no-repeat memory once shaken back in, no group/team split, nothing to project, and the teacher's hand is a plausible source of bias. Beat sticks on speed-to-first-spin and on visible fairness, not on features.

competitors.name: Streamlabs / StreamElements spin-wheel widgets + OBS browser-source wheels (WheelToChoose, SpinRipple, SpinWheelify, StreamSpell)
competitors.model: Free within the streaming platform; several third-party ones advertise 'no login needed' and 'CSPRNG randomness' as the pitch.
competitors.note: Owns the stream half of the use case because it lives inside OBS as a browser source with a chat command (!spin) and a transparent background. Weak: tied to a platform account, styling is locked to the widget's template, and offline/local use is not a concept. That third-party ones lead with 'no signup' and 'provably random' tells you exactly what streamers are shopping for.

complaints.complaint: "I love it the only problem I have is the constant ads after I leave it — it doesn't need to be like YouTube with the constant having to x out of it, it's annoying and repetitive." And: "I have to watch an ad every time I'm done using a spinner."
complaints.source: Apple App Store reviews, Spin The Wheel - Random Picker (id 1467343690), 5★ and 3★, pulled live from the iTunes customer-reviews RSS 2026-08-09
complaints.weWinIf: Zero ads, ever — and specifically zero post-spin interstitials. The moment after a spin is when the audience is looking at the screen; that is the single worst place to put an ad and every competitor puts one there. Make 'no ad has ever appeared here' a stated promise on the page, not just an absence.

complaints.complaint: "I paid to remove ads but they're still popping up? Isn't this breach of contract?" and "I actually purchased both a subscription and the $1.99 to go premium and nothing in the app would unlock. I hit restore purchases again and again and nothing."
complaints.source: Apple App Store reviews, Random - Randomizer Wheel (id 1435808497), 1★
complaints.weWinIf: There is nothing to purchase and nothing to restore, so this failure class cannot exist. Say it plainly: no purchases, no entitlements, no 'restore' button that does nothing.

complaints.complaint: "Used to be free, now they want a subscription for 3 dollars a week to spin a wheel. I'm good lol" / "I've had this app for over 2 years... I wrote wheels with over 2000 items and then one day I open the app and it told me to pay a price I definitely can't pay... it went from 5 stars to 1 star in 1 update." / "You should be sued... I paid for the app two years ago for no ads" and now there's a subscription.
complaints.source: Apple App Store reviews, Spin Wheel Decisions (id 1482510249), 1★ — a dense cluster of them on one review page
complaints.weWinIf: Publish a dated, plain-English no-paywall-ever line in the app itself (not buried in a privacy page), and make the user's data portable by default so the promise is enforceable rather than trust-based: they can export their wheels and walk away at any time. This is the loudest, angriest, most specific complaint in the entire category and it is free for us to win.

complaints.complaint: "You can't even put ten options without paying for 'premium' — just use a free wheel online." / "It won't let you add more then 5 things on the wheel." / "I don't like that you can only have one wheel... me and my friends are doing who gets to pay at dinner and we couldn't even put all the names."
complaints.source: Apple App Store reviews, Spin Wheel Decisions (id 1482510249), 1★
complaints.weWinIf: Unlimited entries and unlimited saved wheels, and say the word 'unlimited' where a first-time user sees it. Also handle the consequence: a 200-name wheel must stay legible (see table stakes), because 'unlimited' that renders as unreadable slivers is a broken promise.

complaints.complaint: "I was enjoying using this app for about 3 weeks then when I went to use it today my wheels disappeared. I'm not going to redo my wheels again. No thanks."
complaints.source: Apple App Store review, Spin The Wheel - Random Picker (id 1467343690), 3★
complaints.weWinIf: Local-only storage makes this risk worse, not better, so we must over-engineer around it: autosave every edit, an explicit Export all wheels to a file button that a teacher can drop in Drive, matching Import, and a visible warning that clearing site data wipes wheels. Ship the backup affordance on day one — a lost class roster is the one bug that loses a teacher permanently.

complaints.complaint: "Enjoying it but the 'recently spun' list never works. I would like to not keep spinning the same options." And: "The wheel is only good for ten rounds, so if you have more than ten items you'll go into repeat purgatory... it wouldn't be so bad if the spin wasn't so long. If you're just gonna give me the same names three times in a row it could at least go faster."
complaints.source: Apple App Store reviews, id 1467343690 (4★) and Random - Randomizer Wheel id 1435808497 (2★)
complaints.weWinIf: Elimination / no-repeat is not an advanced setting, it is the primary classroom mode — make it a toggle on the main screen, show the already-picked names greyed on the wheel rather than deleted, keep a visible 'X of 28 left' counter, and give a one-tap Reset for next period. Also: let the user shorten the spin. Long spin + repeat result is the compounding insult.

complaints.complaint: "The spinner is always on the same spot for every reset and I get the same result too often so I'll be looking for a different app." Plus the community suspicion: r/AskPC "Can Streamers rig Wheel of Names?" — "everytime they spin, mostly the names that win are the same set of names" — and an r/UnethicalLifeProTips thread that shares an actual rigging trick for Wheel of Names.
complaints.source: App Store 3★ (id 1467343690); reddit.com/r/AskPC/comments/xz6w94/ and reddit.com/r/UnethicalLifeProTips/comments/1d71tpu/ (titles and snippets via DuckDuckGo — I could not open the threads themselves)
complaints.weWinIf: Two moves. Mechanically: use crypto.getRandomValues, and randomize the wheel's resting rotation before every spin so the visual start position differs each time — the perception bug is caused by always starting at the same angle. Socially: an optional on-screen session log of every result with a timestamp, plus a short 'how this picks' explainer. A streamer can point chat at the log; a teacher can prove they didn't pick favorites. Note that competitors already advertise 'CSPRNG' and 'provably random' — this is a live purchase criterion, not a nicety.

complaints.complaint: "I can't import lists to use. So I spend a lot of time typing in names for PTA drawings. It's exhausting and creates many chances for human error. I would really love to see an option to import a spreadsheet." And: "You have to enter each item on the list one by one? This doesn't make much sense for people who have hundreds of items."
complaints.source: Apple App Store reviews, Random - Randomizer Wheel (id 1435808497), 3★ and 1★
complaints.weWinIf: The very first interaction should be a big textarea, not an 'add entry +' row. Accept a pasted spreadsheet column and split on newlines, commas, semicolons and tabs; strip empties; dedupe with a visible 'removed 2 duplicates' note the user can undo; show a live count. Typing names one at a time in front of a class is the thing that makes a teacher close the tab.

complaints.complaint: "Why doesn't the name pop up big after spinning? When I clicked the app, the wheel did that — it spun and whatever it landed on appeared big and was displayed. Now that I've purchased it, that doesn't happen... that's what I need, so people see the name pop up."
complaints.source: Apple App Store review, Random - Randomizer Wheel (id 1435808497), 3★
complaints.weWinIf: The winner reveal is the product. Full-bleed card, name at 8–12vw, held until dismissed, readable from the back of a classroom and at OBS overlay scale. Never shrink it, never put anything over it, and make sure it is what a screen reader announces too.

complaints.complaint: "Rate us prompt comes up everytime. Ruins the app." / "I hate this app because every time I try and use it it says rate our app 😡" — multiple reviewers whose only complaint is the nag.
complaints.source: Apple App Store reviews, Spin The Wheel - Raffle App (id 1618397013), 1★–3★
complaints.weWinIf: Absolute no-interruption rule: no rating prompt, no newsletter modal, no onboarding tour, no cookie banner (we collect nothing, so there is nothing to consent to), and critically no dialog can ever open while a spin is running or a winner is displayed. The tip link is a quiet persistent link, never a modal.

complaints.complaint: "The updates to this app has created the need for multiple clicks to actually get to the saved wheels. It is quite annoying to have to click multiple times to get to the desired result." Related: "Seems like a great app but it won't let you click any of the templates or delete any of the wheels" and "it won't let me delete some of my wheels and it's taking up room."
complaints.source: Apple App Store reviews, Spin Wheel Decisions (id 1482510249) 3★, Decision Maker (id 1472904065) 3★, id 1467343690 4★
complaints.weWinIf: Open spin-ready: restore the last-used wheel and put a live SPIN button under the thumb/cursor on load. Saved wheels are one tap from there. And make delete/rename/duplicate work obviously and immediately — broken CRUD on saved wheels is a recurring complaint across three different apps, which suggests it is genuinely easy to get wrong.

complaints.complaint: Typing a class roster into a third-party site is a student-data question: Wheel of Names stores cloud wheels in Google Firestore, and FERPA/GDPR guidance pushes schools toward data minimization and district approval before sending student information to outside vendors. Separately, the existence of a whole cottage industry of 'wheel of names alternative if blocked at school' domains (wheelnames.org, classroulette.com, wheelof-names.com, wheel-ofnames.com) is direct evidence that school content filters block these sites often enough to be a routine classroom failure.
complaints.source: wheelofnames.com/faq (Firestore storage); studentprivacy.ed.gov guidance on school/vendor data sharing; DuckDuckGo results for school-blocked wheel alternatives
complaints.weWinIf: Two concrete deliverables, not a vibe. (1) One sentence at the top of the page a teacher can screenshot for IT: 'Names you type stay in this browser. Nothing is uploaded, no account, no analytics.' Consider a copyable one-paragraph blurb formatted for a district tool-request form. (2) Actually work when the network is filtered or dead — install as a PWA, cache everything, show an 'Offline ready' badge. Being the wheel that still spins when the Wi-Fi dies is a memorable, repeatable reason a teacher picks us permanently.

tableStakes: Bulk paste entry as the primary input — one big textarea that splits on newline/comma/tab, trims blanks, dedupes with an undoable notice, and shows a live entry count. Per-item 'add +' rows as the only input reads amateur instantly.

Multiple named wheels that persist across reload and across sessions, with rename, duplicate and delete that actually work. A teacher has 5 sections; a streamer has 'game night', 'sub goals', 'punishments'.

Elimination / no-repeat mode with picked names shown greyed on the wheel rather than removed, an 'X of 28 left' counter, and a one-tap reset. Plus remove-one-entry inline (the absent kid) without rebuilding the list.
Weighted entries or repeat-count per entry — both Wheel of Names and Picker Wheel have it, so its absence is a visible feature gap even though most users never touch it.

A fullscreen presentation mode with all chrome gone, and a winner reveal at genuinely huge type. This is what makes it projector-legible and OBS-usable; a wheel in a page frame with a sidebar is a toy.
Sound effects with a mute toggle whose state persists. Both a silent-classroom and a stream-audio-mix requirement; forgetting the mute state between spins is a real-world embarrassment.
Session pick history — an ordered list of who came up, copyable as text. Doubles as the fairness receipt and as the 'who still owes an answer' record.

Legibility at scale: a 100+ entry wheel must not degrade into unreadable slivers. Truncate/rotate labels, drop labels below a size threshold, or switch above N entries to a compact reveal that still animates. 'Unlimited entries' is a lie if 60 names are illegible.
Per-segment color control, or at minimum a palette that guarantees adjacent segments differ in both hue and lightness so labels stay readable and colorblind users can still parse the wheel.
Export and import: download all wheels as a file the user owns, import it back, and copy the current list as plain text. With local-only storage this is not a power feature, it is the backup story.
differentiators: The IT-approval sentence. One line at the top — 'Names you type stay in this browser. Nothing is uploaded. No account, no analytics.' — plus a copyable paragraph formatted for a district software-request form. No competitor can write this sentence: Wheel of Names puts cloud wheels in Firestore, Picker Wheel needs an account for persistence, Classroomscreen is a vendor with seats. This is the single most defensible thing we have and it costs one paragraph.

Spins when the Wi-Fi is dead. Installable PWA, fully cached, with a visible 'Offline ready' badge once it is. School networks filter and drop constantly (hence the whole ecosystem of 'wheel of names if blocked' mirror domains), and a streamer's PC is often network-saturated. Being the one that never fails mid-lesson is how a teacher stops shopping.

Fairness receipts. crypto.getRandomValues, a randomized resting angle before every spin (this alone kills the #1 perceived-unfairness complaint), and an optional on-screen session log with timestamps. Streamers can point chat at it; teachers can prove they didn't pick favorites. Competitors already market 'CSPRNG' and 'provably random', so this is a live buying criterion — we just do it honestly and show the evidence.

Reduced-motion honesty. Honor prefers-reduced-motion with a dignified alternative reveal (a quick shuffle-and-settle, no rotation), cap any celebratory flash under 3 flashes/second per WCAG 2.3.x, and make confetti opt-in. A classroom of 28 statistically contains kids with vestibular sensitivity, migraine and photosensitivity. Nobody in this category treats a spinning disc as the accessibility problem it is; being the one that does is both right and quotable.

Class-day ergonomics as a first-class mode: an 'absent today' toggle that greys a name for the session without deleting it, and a 'Reset for next period' button. Teachers currently solve this by deleting names and retyping them the next day — that is the daily papercut nobody has addressed.

Two one-click presets on first run instead of a settings safari. Classroom: elimination on, sound off, maximum type, high-contrast projector palette. Stream: transparent background for OBS browser source (plus a chroma-green option), spacebar spin hotkey, compact overlay layout. The same core app, aimed twice.

Degrade gracefully to paper. Print the list as cut-up slips, and print a numbered roster. It sounds unglamorous, but it is the move that says we understand the popsicle-stick user rather than trying to beat them — and it makes the app useful on a day the projector bulb dies.

Group and team split, not just single-name pick. Flippity has it (lineups, groups up to 15, teams up to 15) and it is the one feature teachers reliably leave a wheel app to go get. Adding 'split these 28 names into 7 groups of 4' to a picker is cheap client-side work and closes the main reason a teacher keeps two tools open.

aesthetic.categoryConventions:
Today the category looks like a carnival midway crossed with a slot machine: 6–12 fully saturated rainbow segments, glossy 3D bevels and inner shadows on the disc, a drop-shadowed plastic pointer, a coin-drop or game-show ding, and a confetti burst on win. Mobile apps push further into gamification — coin economies, unlockable skins, template galleries, 'watch an ad for 40 coins.' The older web incumbents (Wheel Decide, Flippity) look frozen around 2014: chunky beveled buttons, cramped type, banner ad slots framing the wheel on three sides. Wheel of Names is the modern-ish benchmark — flat disc, clean sans, competent motion physics — but its page is still fundamentally an ad frame wrapped around a settings sidebar.

Reads DATED right now: gloss/bevel/inner-shadow 3D wheels; skeuomorphic pointers with drop shadows; the default rainbow (pure red next to pure green next to pure blue); Comic Sans and bubbly rounded 'teacher clipart' display faces; animated confetti/firework GIFs; dark-red casino felt backgrounds; anything that looks like it wants to be a slot machine.

Reads CURRENT: a flat or very subtly elevated disc; one confident accent hue with a deliberately tuned multi-hue segment ramp rather than a rainbow; generous whitespace around the wheel so it is the only busy object on screen; large, restrained typography; a deceleration curve that feels physically convincing rather than a linear ease-out; and full-bleed, typographic reveal states instead of decorated popups. Restraint everywhere except the winner moment, which should be unapologetically big.
aesthetic.emotionalContext:
There are two users and they are more alike than they look: both are performing in front of an audience, in real time, with zero tolerance for friction, and for both the failure mode is social embarrassment rather than data loss.

The teacher is STANDING, 8–12 feet from a washed-out projector or a wall-mounted panel, room lights on, 28 kids watching, mid-lesson. They have roughly six seconds before the room's attention breaks. They cannot squint, cannot troubleshoot, cannot let an unvetted ad image appear in front of children, and absolutely cannot be asked to log in in front of the class. They are often tapping a touch panel while half-facing the room, so they are aiming badly. And the whole social purpose of the tool is to look fair — the point is that the picked student believes it wasn't personal.

The streamer is SEATED in a dark room, wheel on a second monitor or as an OBS browser source, live, with a chat that is primed to shout 'rigged.' They need it readable at overlay scale, transparent-background friendly, triggerable without alt-tabbing away from the game, and silent unless they choose otherwise.

Design consequences, concretely: minimum body text ~18px and controls ~48px because of the standing-and-aiming-badly problem; winner type at 8–12vw; contrast tuned for projector washout, meaning near-black or near-white labels on their own segment fills, never a brand-tinted mid-gray on a mid-tone fill; no modal may EVER open during a spin or over a winner; the app opens spin-ready with the last wheel restored, because setup time is the moment the class goes feral. Warm rather than clinical — this is supposed to be a small piece of fun — but grown-up enough that a teacher isn't embarrassed to project it and a streamer isn't embarrassed to overlay it.
aesthetic.recommendedFeel: Warm, playful-but-grown-up, high-contrast, fair/trustworthy, theatrical, calm-celebratory. Think a small stage with a good spotlight — not a casino floor, not a kindergarten bulletin board.

colorRecommendation.hueFamily: Deep aubergine/plum as the identity ground (something around #2A1A33 to #3B2547), with marigold as the single accent (pointer, winner card, tip link), and a warm analogous segment ramp — marigold → apricot → coral → rose → magenta — anchored by two or three cool segments (teal, periwinkle) so no two neighbours share a lightness.
colorRecommendation.rationale: Plum is the theatre-curtain-and-spotlight colour. It carries the 'let fate decide' showmanship the category wants without any of the casino-red or slot-machine-gold baggage, and its deep value keeps it adult enough to project in a classroom or drop on a stream overlay without looking childish. Practically it does real work: a dark plum canvas makes the wheel the only bright object on a washed-out projector, which gives you exactly the focal hierarchy you want, and light segment fills on a deep ground survive projector gamma far better than pastels on white. Marigold is the highest-contrast complement to plum, so the pointer and the winner card read instantly from the back row — and it means the winner is not marked in red (which reads as error/wrong) or green (which in a classroom reads as 'correct', and a random pick is not a correctness judgement; a picked student should never feel scored). Build the segment ramp by index-with-stride so adjacent wedges always differ in both hue and lightness, and verify labels at 4.5:1 against their own fill. Within a 23-app portfolio deep plum is very likely still open: indigo/navy is where every utility defaults, teal and green get claimed by checklist and organiser apps, and warm terracotta/amber tends to go to the domestic ones (Home Inventory, Baby Log).
colorRecommendation.avoid: Casino red + gold on black felt — beyond being a cliché, gambling styling is exactly the visual signature that gets a domain flagged by school content filters, which is a genuine distribution risk for half our audience, and it reads badly to parents. The full-saturation default rainbow — it is the single strongest signal of 'generic free wheel', it wrecks label contrast wherever adjacent segments share a lightness, and it is unparseable for the roughly 8% of boys in any classroom with red-green colour deficiency. Blue as primary — it is the portfolio default and emotionally wrong here (blue is calm and corporate; this moment is small-theatre). Green as the winner colour, for the 'correct answer' misread. Pure #000 or pure #FFF grounds with thin type, because projector gamma crushes both — use an off-black plum and an off-white. Neon/cyberpunk glow and heavy drop shadows, which date fast and smear at overlay scale. And Comic Sans or any bubbly rounded display face: it signals 'for small children', which alienates the streamer half and reads amateur to teachers.

confidence:
MEDIUM-HIGH overall, with an important methodology caveat.

METHODOLOGY CAVEAT: this session's WebSearch budget was already exhausted (200/200) before I began, so I could not use the search tool at all. Everything here came from (a) direct page fetches, (b) DuckDuckGo's HTML endpoint used as a search substitute, and (c) live curl calls to Apple's public APIs. That last channel is the strongest evidence in this report.

HIGH CONFIDENCE — verified from primary sources on 2026-08-09:
- The iOS competitor set, star ratings and rating counts (iTunes Search API, live): Spin The Wheel - Random Picker 4.87★/93,693; Tiny Decisions 4.71★/89,295; Spin Wheel Decisions 4.48★/18,902; Wheel+ 4.78★/11,603; Spin The Wheel Spinner Picker 4.54★/10,169.
- Every verbatim complaint quoted above. These were pulled from Apple's customer-reviews RSS for app IDs 1467343690, 1472904065, 1482510249, 1435808497 and 1618397013 and filtered to 1–3 stars. They are real review text, not paraphrase.
- Picker Wheel pricing ($5 / $10 / $25 per month; free tier 15 files, 3 AI queries/day) read directly off pickerwheel.com/plan.
- Classroomscreen pricing ($0 Basic with a 3-saved-name-list cap, $3/mo or $36/yr Pro, $525/yr for 25 seats) read directly off classroomscreen.com/pricing.
- Wheel of Names' model: ad-supported, session-dismissible ads, 'We do not take any form of payments or donations from users', cloud wheels stored in Google Firestore — read off wheelofnames.com and its FAQ.

COULD NOT VERIFY — treat with caution:
- REDDIT IS UNREAD. reddit.com blocks both my fetcher and its own JSON endpoint from this environment (403 on both www and old). The two Reddit items I cite — r/UnethicalLifeProTips 'Rigged Wheel of Names, non random name picker' (1d71tpu) and r/AskPC 'Can Streamers rig Wheel of Names?' (xz6w94) including the 'everytime they spin, mostly the names that win are the same set of names' line — come from DuckDuckGo result snippets, not from reading the threads. Titles and gist are solid; surrounding discussion, upvotes and any rebuttals are unknown.
- ANDROID SENTIMENT IS INFERRED, NOT OBSERVED. Google Play listings render via JS and the fetch was blocked, and Play has no equivalent public review feed. Every verbatim quote here is iOS. I'd expect Android to skew more ad-heavy, not less, but I did not confirm it.
- wheelofnames.com traffic (~9.6M monthly visitors / ~19M visits, US rank ~1,098) came from third-party traffic-estimator snippets via DuckDuckGo. Order-of-magnitude only; do not put a specific number in any copy.
- THE FERPA/PRIVACY ANGLE IS A HYPOTHESIS, NOT A DOCUMENTED MASS COMPLAINT. I found no teacher forum thread of people objecting to typing rosters into wheel sites. What I found is (i) legitimate FERPA/GDPR data-minimisation guidance from studentprivacy.ed.gov about school-vendor data sharing, and (ii) real, indirect evidence that school filtering blocks these sites — an entire cluster of 'wheel of names alternative if blocked' mirror domains exists. So 'works offline / never blocked' is well-supported; 'district IT will care about the names' is a defensible legal argument I'd test with one teacher before making it the headline.
- No Trustpilot or G2 presence worth citing exists for this category; it is too small and too consumer. I looked and found nothing usable.
- The 'what reads dated vs current' design read is my synthesis from examining the incumbents' own pages plus stock-imagery and Dribbble result descriptions. It is a designer's judgement call, not a cited survey — weigh it as opinion.
- Picker Wheel's and Spin Wheel Decisions' exact current subscription prices may have drifted; the $3/week and $15/month figures for Spin Wheel Decisions come from user reviews (which are dated and may predate changes), not from the App Store listing itself.
